text: In July 2007, the bookseller Borders moved The Adventures of Tintin in the Congo by Hergé to an area reserved for adult graphic novels, and Waterstone's followed suit. In 2007, the Brooklyn Public Library removed the book from public display and kept it locked in a back room. In August 2007 a student filed a complaint in Brussels demanding a ban, and in February 2012 the court ruled that the book would not be banned. In September 2011 the book was removed from a children's library in Kulturhuset in Stockholm.

sources.quote: The CRE called on bookshops to remove the comic; responding that it was committed to letting its "customers make the choice", Borders moved the book to an area reserved for adult graphic novels. UK bookseller Waterstone's followed suit.

sources.quote: In August 2007, Congolese student Bienvenu Mbutu Mondondo filed a complaint in Brussels, claiming that Tintin in the Congo was an insult to the Congolese people that should be banned. Public prosecutors initiated a criminal case although the matter was transferred to a civil court in April 2010.

text: Sophie's Choice by William Styron was banned in Lebanon for its positive depiction of Jews. In November 1979, censors working for the government of South Africa under apartheid banned it for being a sexually explicit work. In 2002 the Norwalk-La Mirada High School District pulled it from the La Mirada High School Library in California because of a parent's complaint about its sexual content.

text: The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir was banned in its Spanish-language translation, printed in Argentina, in Francoist Spain in 1955. In 1956, the Vatican placed The Second Sex on the Index librorum prohibitorum, its index of prohibited books, where it remained until the policy of prohibition was abolished in 1966.
